body:
What is Kush? It's a family of cannabis strains named for the Hindu Kush, a mountain range in Afghanistan and Pakistan where local cannabis has long been grown for hashish. Today "Kush" appears in many strain names, and it's also casual slang for cannabis in general. Here's where the name comes from, how those genetics reached the West, and what the name can and can't tell you.

## What is Kush? Its roots in the Hindu Kush

The Hindu Kush is a mountain system about 500 miles (800 km) long. It begins at the Pamirs, near where the borders of Afghanistan, China and Pakistani-administered Kashmir meet, and runs southwest through Pakistan into Afghanistan. Its highest peak, Tirich Mir, rises 25,230 feet.

Farmers there kept local cannabis varieties going for generations, the kind of long-established strains growers call landraces. Afghan plants grown for hashish caught botanists' attention, and early classifiers described them as short, densely branched plants with broad leaflets.

## Indica, sativa or hybrid?

Kush strains are usually sold as indica or as hybrids that lean indica, because 20th-century botanists used Afghan hashish plants as their model for Cannabis indica. That short, bushy, broad-leaf look became the popular picture of an indica.

Genetics tell a messier story. A 2021 study that genotyped more than 100 cannabis samples found that plants labeled sativa and indica were genetically indistinct across the genome. An earlier study of 30 dispensary strains likewise found no clear genetic support for the indica, sativa and hybrid categories. So "indica" on a Kush label reflects tradition, not reliable genetics or a promised effect. Our guide to [indica vs. sativa](/blog/indica-vs-sativa/) explains the labels in depth.

## Kush as everyday slang

So what does kush mean in everyday talk? It has become casual shorthand for cannabis in general, often with a hint of quality, and you'll hear it in music and everyday talk about flower with no Kush genetics at all. Our roundup of [other names for cannabis](/blog/other-names-for-marijuana/) covers more of the vocabulary.

## How Kush genetics traveled west in the 1960s and 1970s

The story usually told goes like this: in the 1960s and 1970s, young Western travelers crossed Afghanistan on the overland route nicknamed the Hippie Trail, and some carried cannabis seeds home. Growers in North America and Europe then bred those plants, prizing their compact size and resin. Firm records are scarce, so take the details as lore. Whatever the route, Afghan-type plants left a mark: their short, bushy shape suits indoor growing, and "Kush" turns up in the names of many later strains.

## OG Kush and the 1990s

OG Kush is the family's breakout strain. Most accounts date its fame to the early 1990s, first in South Florida and then in Los Angeles, where it became a West Coast favorite. Its parentage is disputed, and even the meaning of "OG" has several competing explanations. Our guide to [what OG means](/blog/what-does-og-mean/) sorts through the stories.

## Common Kush traits: aroma, bud structure and reported effects

- **Aroma:** often described as earthy, woody or piney, with spicy, hashy or fuel-like notes.
- **Bud structure:** dense, chunky flowers, frequently with a heavy frosting of trichomes.
- **Reported effects:** many people describe Kush as relaxing and body-focused, but experiences vary with the plant, the dose and the person.

Think of these as tendencies, not promises, since Kush crosses can lean in very different directions.

## Well-known Kush strains

A few Kush names come up often:

- **Hindu Kush:** named straight for the mountains and often sold as a classic, landrace-style line
- **OG Kush:** the 1990s strain behind a large family of "OG" crosses
- **Bubba Kush:** often described as heavy and earthy-sweet
- **Purple Kush:** known for its purple hues; researchers have even used a sequenced Purple Kush genome to build genetic markers for studying other strains

These are examples, not a list of what's in stock; selection varies by store and changes often. Our look at [notable strains this year](/blog/top-cannabis-strains-of-2026/) shows what's catching attention now.

## Shopping tip: read the lab data, not just the name

A strain name is only a clue. In one genetic study, most strains had at least one genetic outlier when bought from different dispensaries, so two jars with the same Kush name can look, smell and feel different.

So read the label: check the THC and CBD figures, look at any terpenes listed, and ask our budtenders what they're noticing in a particular batch. When you're ready, [browse your store's menu](/shop/) to see what's available today. Kush or not, it's for adults 21 and older; please consume responsibly.

faq.q: What does Kush usually smell like?
faq.a: Kush is usually described as earthy, woody or piney, often with a spicy, hashy or fuel-like edge, and some crosses lean sweet. Those notes come from terpenes, which vary from plant to plant and batch to batch. Smell is personal, so compare the terpenes listed on labels and ask a budtender which batches stand out.

faq.q: How is Kush different from OG Kush?
faq.a: Kush is the broad family name, rooted in plants from the Hindu Kush region. OG Kush is one specific strain within that family; by most accounts, it rose to fame in the 1990s, first in Florida and then in California. Its exact parentage is disputed, and even the "OG" in its name has several competing explanations.

faq.q: Are Kush strains stronger than others?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Potency depends on the individual plant, how it was grown and how fresh it is, not on the word Kush in the name. Some Kush strains test high and some don't, and the same name can vary from grower to grower. Check the THC figure on the label rather than going by the name.

review.summary: 20 claims checked: 19 ok, 1 overstated (fixed: FAQ stated the OG Kush origin story as fact); 1 ok claim got a precision edit (the range's eastern end, worded as Britannica words a disputed border area). All four sources reopened and support the text.

claims.claim: Kush strains are named for the Hindu Kush, a mountain range about 500 miles (800 km) long in Afghanistan and Pakistan (takeaway 1, intro, section 1)
claims.source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Hindu-Kush (curl with a browser user agent, 2026-10-24): "a large mountain system in Central Asia, approximately 500 miles (800 km) long"

claims.claim: The range runs "from the Pamirs near the Pakistan-China border through Pakistan into Afghanistan"
claims.fix: precision edit: now "begins at the Pamirs, near where the borders of Afghanistan, China and Pakistani-administered Kashmir meet, and runs southwest through Pakistan into Afghanistan" (the brief bars political framing of the region; this follows Britannica's wording)
claims.source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Hindu-Kush: "To the east the Hindu Kush buttresses the Pamir range near the point where the borders of China, Pakistani-administered Kashmir, and Afghanistan meet, after which it runs southwest through Pakistan and into Afghanistan"

claims.claim: The highest peak, Tirich Mir, rises 25,230 feet
claims.source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Hindu-Kush: "Mount Tirich Mir, which rises to 25,230 feet (7,690 meters)"

claims.claim: Local cannabis has long been grown there for hashish; long-established local strains are called landraces
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6225593/ (full text via Europe PMC): "Vavilov assigned the taxon C. sativa to plants cultivated in Afghanistan for hashish"

claims.claim: Early classifiers described Afghan hashish plants as short, densely branched, with broad leaflets
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6225593/: "Schultes et al. assigned the taxon C. indica to Afghani plants, and described the taxon having broad, oblanceolate leaflets, densely branched ... and very short (< 1.3 m)"

claims.claim: Kush is usually sold as indica or indica-leaning because 20th-century botanists used Afghan hashish plants as their model for Cannabis indica (takeaway 2)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6225593/: Anderson "typified C. indica with plants that Schultes described in Afghanistan"; vernacular "Indica" is "typified by plants from Afghanistan"; this skewing gave rise to "today's vernacular taxonomy of 'Sativa' and 'Indica'"

claims.claim: A 2021 study genotyped more than 100 samples and found sativa- and indica-labeled plants genetically indistinct across the genome (takeaway 2)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8516649/ (abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 34650264): "Analysis of over 100 Cannabis samples ... genotyped for over 100,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms indicated that Sativa- and Indica-labelled samples were genetically indistinct on a genome-wide scale"

claims.claim: An earlier study of 30 dispensary strains found no clear genetic support for indica, sativa and hybrid categories
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7815053/ (abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 33526091): "30 strains obtained from dispensaries in three states"; "We failed to find clear genetic support for commonly referenced Sativa, Indica and Hybrid types"
